client: I've been having a really hard time since my breakup with Maria about three months ago, and I guess that's why I finally decided to come here. I used to love going hiking with my friends on weekends, but lately I just can't bring myself to enjoy it — or anything, really. I'm not even sure therapy can fix something like this, but I figured I had nothing to lose by trying.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up here, especially when you're feeling this low and uncertain about whether anything can help — I'm really glad you came. What you're describing, losing the joy in things you used to love like hiking, is such a painful and common part of grief after a significant relationship ends, and it makes complete sense that you're struggling. I'm curious — when you imagine yourself back on one of those hiking trails, what thoughts or feelings come up for you?

client: When I picture myself out on a trail, the first thing that hits me is this image of Maria — we did that route together so many times, and now it just feels like it belongs to her somehow. I get this hollow, almost sick feeling in my chest, like I'd just be surrounded by reminders of what I lost. Honestly, I think part of me avoids it because being out there alone would just make the loneliness feel even more real.
therapist: That hollow, sick feeling you're describing makes so much sense — those trails hold real memories, and your mind is trying to protect you from that pain by keeping you away. I want to gently notice something with you though: you mentioned going with *friends*, which means you wouldn't actually be alone out there, yet part of your mind seems to be framing it that way. What do you think it would feel like to test that thought — that being on the trail means facing loneliness — by going once with someone you trust?

client: I hear what you're saying, and yeah, logically I know my friends would be there — but I'm not sure it would actually feel any different. Like, even when I'm around people lately, I still feel this weird distance, this sense that nobody really gets what I'm going through with Maria. I guess I'm worried that going on the hike and still feeling lonely would somehow be worse than just staying home.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — it feels safer to avoid the test than to risk "failing" it and feeling even more hopeless. What you're describing, feeling distant even in a crowd, often comes from a belief that you have to carry this grief invisibly, which can quietly deepen the loneliness. I'm wondering — have you been able to tell any of your friends even a little bit of what you just shared with me, about how much you're struggling since the breakup?

client: Not really, honestly. I've kind of just been saying "I'm fine" or deflecting with jokes when they ask how I'm doing, because I don't want to be that guy who can't get over a breakup three months later. I guess I worry they'll think I'm being dramatic, or that they'll get tired of hearing about it.
therapist: It's so understandable that you want to protect yourself from judgment, but I notice there's an automatic thought worth examining here: "three months is too long to still be hurting," as if grief has a deadline your friends are secretly tracking. The irony is that by hiding behind "I'm fine," you're actually creating the very distance that makes you feel unseen and alone. What do you think might happen if you let just one trusted friend see even a small piece of what you're really going through?

client: I mean, maybe you're right that I'm creating some of that distance myself, and that's kind of uncomfortable to sit with. But I think about opening up to someone like my friend Jake, and I just imagine him not knowing what to say, or giving me some generic "she wasn't right for you anyway" response — and that would honestly make me feel worse, not better. I don't know, maybe I've just convinced myself it's safer to keep it inside than to risk that kind of disappointment.
therapist: That anticipation of disappointment is real and worth taking seriously — you've probably experienced moments before where vulnerability didn't land the way you hoped, and your mind is trying to shield you from that. But I gently want to point out that you're essentially making a decision *for* Jake before he's even had the chance to show up for you, which means he never gets the opportunity to surprise you. What do you actually know about Jake that might be worth weighing against that fear — has he ever shown up for you in a meaningful way before?

client: Yeah, actually — when my dad got sick a couple years ago, Jake was the one who kept checking in on me without me even having to ask. I guess I kind of forgot about that when I was picturing him fumbling through some awkward response about Maria. It's just hard because this feels different, more embarrassing somehow, like grief over a relationship is less serious than a family crisis and I should just be over it by now.
therapist: What you just did there is really important — you went looking for evidence and found something that genuinely contradicts the story your mind has been telling you about Jake, and that takes honesty. It's also worth gently challenging this hierarchy of "acceptable" grief you've described, because pain doesn't rank itself by category — a relationship that mattered deeply to you *is* serious, full stop. I'm curious where you think this idea came from, that heartbreak is somehow less deserving of support than other kinds of loss?

client: Honestly, I think a lot of it comes from how I grew up — my dad was pretty stoic, and the message was always kind of "deal with it and move on," especially around relationship stuff. I remember him saying something once about how heartbreak is just part of life and you don't make a big deal out of it. I never really questioned that until just now, but I can see how I've been carrying that around like it's some kind of rule I have to follow.
therapist: That's a really meaningful insight — recognizing that what feels like a personal truth is actually a rule you inherited, one that made sense in your dad's world but may not be serving you now. Carrying that "deal with it silently" message has likely made this grief so much heavier, because you've been fighting the pain *and* judging yourself for having it at the same time. I'm wondering — now that you can see it as something you learned rather than something that's simply true, does it feel like a rule you actually want to keep following?

client: When you put it that way, no, I don't think I actually want to keep following it — it's just that knowing something intellectually and actually changing how you feel about it seem like very different things. Like, I can tell myself "it's okay to struggle after a breakup" but there's still this voice in my head that sounds a lot like my dad saying I'm being weak. I'm not sure how you get from understanding something to actually believing it in your gut.
therapist: You've just named one of the most honest and important things about how change actually works — insight is the map, but it's new *experiences* that rewire the gut feeling, and that takes time and repetition. One way to start bridging that gap is through small moments that gently contradict the old rule, like letting Jake in even briefly, because each time the world responds with care instead of judgment, that inner voice loses a little of its authority. What might it feel like to treat one small act of openness this week — not as a test of whether you're "over it," but as an experiment in gathering new evidence about what you actually deserve?

client: I like the idea of calling it an experiment rather than some big emotional moment I have to get right — that framing actually makes it feel a little less terrifying. But I'm already thinking about how it might go, like maybe I text Jake and he's busy or gives a one-word response, and then I've put myself out there for nothing. I guess I'm just scared that even a small step could end up feeling like more proof that I should've kept things to myself.
therapist: It's really telling that your mind is already writing Jake's response for him — and notably, it's writing the worst version, which is exactly what that old "stay stoic, stay safe" rule would want you to believe to keep you protected. Even a busy or brief reply wouldn't actually prove you shouldn't have reached out; it would just mean Jake was busy, and those are two very different things. What would you say to a close friend who was afraid to reach out because they might get an imperfect response — would you tell them that silence was the safer choice?

client: No, I'd probably tell them to just send the message and that an imperfect response is better than wondering forever — it's kind of annoying how clearly I can see that when it's hypothetically someone else's problem. I think I'd feel pretty hypocritical saying "stay silent" to a friend when I know that's not actually good advice. I guess the hard part is that I can be compassionate toward some imaginary friend way more easily than I can toward myself.
therapist: What you just noticed — that gap between how you'd treat a friend versus how you treat yourself — is actually one of the most important things we can work with in therapy, and the fact that you can see it so clearly is a real strength. That double standard isn't a character flaw; it's something that was taught to you, by that same stoic voice that said struggle should be private and silent. What do you think it would take to become even a little bit more like that compassionate friend to yourself — not perfectly, just enough to send one honest message to Jake this week?
